title: Poets close
hook: the poets close, from Konya to Amherst, with Bede's cowherd who sang: poems are made for the ear
tomorrow: a monk practiced so hard his feet bled. what did the Buddha ask him?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: my anthology. A garland with every poet named, and honey you carry inside. Today the poets close, and the anthology gets a voice.

Some people leave the room when the karaoke mic starts coming around the table. Caedmon was one of them. The monk-historian Bede tells it. At feasts near the abbey of Whitby, a harp went from hand to hand, and everyone sang in turn. Whenever Caedmon saw it coming, he got up and went home, ashamed, because he couldn't sing. One night he slipped out to the cattle shed, his job that night, and fell asleep. Someone stood beside him in a dream and said: Caedmon, sing me something.
screen: `THE MIC COMES AROUND.` → `THE HARP AT THE FEAST.` → `HE SLIPS OUT TO THE CATTLE.` → `CAEDMON, SING ME SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: I can't sing, he said. That's why I left. Sing anyway, said the stranger. Sing the beginning of created things. And Caedmon sang, in his own tongue, verses praising God the Maker that he had never heard before. In the morning he was taken to the abbess Hilda. Learned people listened, then read passages of scripture to him to see what he would do. He went away, and came back with them turned into song. Bede's picture for it is homely: like a clean animal chewing the cud. Here is the teaching under it. In Christian monastic life, sacred words were taken in by ear and turned over aloud, again and again, the way a cow ruminates. Paul says faith comes by hearing, and monks read in murmurs and sang their psalms instead of skimming them. A word said aloud passes through your breath and your body before it reaches your mind. The poets in this block can be taken in the same way. Rumi's verses in Konya were recited and sung. Hafiz is recited at his tomb. Every one of them, right through to Dickinson in Amherst, can be given a voice. So the way to close the poets isn't to file them. It's to give one of them your breath, and someone else's ear.
screen: `SING THE BEGINNING OF CREATED THINGS.` · `SCRIPTURE READ TO HIM, TURNED TO SONG.` · `LIKE A CLEAN ANIMAL CHEWING THE CUD.` · `FAITH COMES BY HEARING.` · then, large: `READ IT ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Choose one poem from your anthology and read it aloud to someone, in the room or on the phone. If no one's near, read it to the room, slowly, and listen to how it sounds in your own voice. Then read it once more, a little slower.
Poets close: the end of the poets, from Konya to Amherst, with Caedmon's lesson that a poem is finished in a voice.
Your line: read it aloud. Caedmon chewed the words over until they became song. Day 1586, and the poets are done.

howItsDone: In monasteries, scripture is read aloud at meals and the psalms are sung in choir; in lectio divina a reader may murmur a passage slowly, turning it over. Poetry readings, recitations at Hafiz's tomb and sung Rumi keep poems in the voice.

fork.setup: your friend's book club only discusses poems they've read silently at home. someone suggests opening each meeting by reading one aloud. what fits Caedmon's story?
options: read it aloud: in Bede's story words are taken in by ear and turned over in the voice.
skip it: hearing a poem adds nothing to reading it carefully on the page.
only if a trained performer reads, so the poem isn't spoiled.
fork.reveal: Caedmon couldn't sing until he did, and he learned scripture by hearing it. A poem said aloud passes through breath and body, not just the eyes.

original.note: Latin: by chewing the cud. Bede's word for how Caedmon turned scripture over into song.

tie.story: Caedmon, who fled the harp, sang in a dream and then turned scripture he heard into song, like an animal chewing the cud.

Caedmon.meaning: a man at Whitby who, Bede says, began singing after a dream

Bede.meaning: an English monk who wrote a history of the English church

Whitby.meaning: an abbey on the coast of northern England

Hilda.meaning: the abbess who led the community at Whitby

Amherst.meaning: the Massachusetts town where Emily Dickinson lived

sources.ref: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People 4.24 (Caedmon: the harp at the feast, the dream, 'sing the beginning of created things', the abbess Hilda, scripture turned to song like a clean animal chewing the cud)
